Direct ab initio calculation of the dynamical matrix

Marek Hyt’ha and Antonín Šimů\overcirc{\text{u}}nek Address:  Institute of Physics of the Czech Academy of Science, Cukrovarnická 10, 162 53 Praha 6, Czech Republic
August 24, 2026
Abstract

In this paper there is presented method for ab initio calculation of the phonon spectra. The method is based upon a direct calculation of the dynamical matrix via second derivatives of the total energy. The pseudopotential technique in plane-wave basis set was used to calculate the total energy within the local density approximation (LDA). For the change of the electron density there is derived the self-consistent equation which is solved analytically with no use of iterations. In this paper the attention is paid only to non-metallic systems.

I Introduction

Increasing accuracy of methods for calculation of the electronic structure of solids enable us to obtain the variety of properties of the solid state. In this paper, there is described new scheme for ab initio calculations of phonon spectra in non-metallic systems.

The problem of phonons as the perturbation of the perfect crystal lattice is used to be studied in different ways. The first one is the so-called direct approach [2, 3] based upon the comparison of the properties of unperturbed and perturbed states. The perturbed state is solved with use of the supercell geometry. This method enable us to study both the linear and nonlinear properties of the crystal lattice. Disadvantage of this method is that for each phonon wavevector 𝐪\bf q we need a corresponding supercell. Only a few phonons can be described by the supercell containing only a few cells, and this is the reason why the use of this method is limited only to few special long-wave phonons. Thus, this supercell technique seems to be insufficient as there are a lot of quantities, which must be computed by integrating over phonon frequencies of the whole Brillouin zone.

The second way is to calculate the dynamical matrix which can describe dynamical properties of solids with use of the linear response methods.

In this paper there is presented method for ab initio calculation of phonon spectra of non-metallic systems. At first the self-consistent electron charge density is calculated. Then, the self-consistent variation of charge density for an arbitrary phonon wave-length is calculated. After that, that one is used for calculating of the dynamical matrix. The presented scheme is restricted to non-metallic systems because the variation of the numbers of states with respect to perturbation in non-metallic systems is almost zero. The situation in metals is more complex.

The presented method differs from the other linear response methods, the dielectric matrix method [4], the method of Baroni et al. [5], the method of King-Smith and Needs [6] and the method of Rignanese, Michenaud and Gonze [7, 8]. The presented method is based on direct calculation of the dynamical matrix via the second derivatives of the total potential energy of the crystal lattice.

Throughout the paper, the hartree units are used.

II Dynamical matrix

In the harmonic approximation the theory of lattice dynamics can be formulated in terms of the dynamical matrix [9]. Then it can be written

[D⁡(𝐪)−ω2​(𝐪)]​W​(𝐪)=𝟎,{\left[{\it D}({\bf q})-\omega^{2}({\bf q})\right]}{\it W}(\bf q)=0, (1)

where D{\it D} stands for the dynamical matrix, 𝐪{\bf q} is the wavevector of the phonon, ω\omega is the frequency of the phonon and W{\it W} is the eigenvector of the dynamical matrix which represents the polarization of the phonon. The dimension of the dynamical matrix is 3​N×3​N{\it 3N\times 3N}, where N{\it N} stands for the number of atoms per cell. Elements of the dynamical matrix can be expressed as [9]

Dα​β(𝐪,μν)=1Mμ​Mν∑𝐡Aα​β(𝐡,μν)exp(−i𝐪⋅𝐡),D_{\alpha\beta}({\bf q},\mu\nu)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{M_{\mu}M_{\nu}}}\sum_{\bf h}A_{\alpha\beta}({{\bf h},\mu\nu})\exp{(-i\bf{q\cdot h})}, (2)

where Mμ,MνM_{\mu},M_{\nu} are masses of atom μ\mu and ν\nu, α\alpha and β\beta are Cartesian directions and 𝐡\bf{h} is vector of the translation symmetry. Elements of the matrix 𝐀\bf{A} are defined as

Aα​β​(𝐡,μ​ν)=d​e​f∂2VL∂uαμ,0​∂uβν,𝐡|𝐮=0,A_{\alpha\beta}({\bf h},{\mu\nu})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle def}}{{=}}\left.\frac{\partial^{2}V_{L}}{\partial{u}_{\alpha}^{\mu,0}\partial{u}_{\beta}^{\nu,{\bf h}}}\right|_{{\bf u}=0}, (3)

where VLV_{L} stands for the total potential energy of the crystal lattice, uαμ,0u_{\alpha}^{\mu,0} is a vector giving displacement of atom μ\mu away from equilibrium in direction of α\alpha axes. The uβν,𝐡u_{\beta}^{\nu,{\bf h}} is a vector of displacement away from equilibrium in the direction of β\beta axes of atom ν\nu in elementary cell with the translation vector 𝐡\bf{h} from the cell containing atom μ\mu. Defining the operator

∂μ,αq=1Mμ∑𝐡e−i𝐪⋅𝐡∂∂uαμ,h|𝐮=0,\partial_{\mu,\alpha}^{q}=\left.\frac{1}{\sqrt{M_{\mu}}}\sum_{\bf h}e^{-i{\bf q}\cdot{\bf h}}\frac{\partial}{\partial u_{\alpha}^{\mu,h}}\right|_{{\bf u}=0}, (4)

one can write the dynamical matrix as

Dα​β(𝐪,μν)=∂μ,αq∗∂ν,βqVL,D_{\alpha\beta}({{\bf q},\mu\nu})=\partial_{\mu,\alpha}^{q*}\partial_{\nu,\beta}^{q}V_{L}, (5)

where asterisk means the complex conjugated operator.

To solve the Eq. (1) we have to know elements of the dynamical matrix. They can be calculated on the basis of elements of matrix A{\it A}. To calculate elements of the matrix A{\it A} we need the second derivatives of energy VLV_{L} for which it can be written

VL=VE​w+Ee​l,V_{L}=V_{Ew}+E_{el}, (6)

where VE​wV_{Ew} is the Ewald ion-ion interaction energy and Ee​l{E}_{el} stands for energy of the set of electrons.

To find the contribution of the VE​wV_{Ew} to the dynamical matrix is easy because the analytical expressions for that one are well known [10] and therefore in the rest of this paper we study only term Ee​lE_{el}.

Using the conventional density functional formalism [1] in the pseudopotential framework, the total energy of the set of electrons is given by [2]

Ee​l\displaystyle E_{el} =\displaystyle= Eε−12​∫ρ⁡(𝐫)​Vc​(𝐫)​d3​r\displaystyle E_{\varepsilon}-\frac{1}{2}\int\rho({\bf r})V_{c}({\bf r})d^{3}r (7)
−\displaystyle- ∫μx​c​(𝐫)​ρ​(𝐫)​d3​r+Ex​c​[ρ],\displaystyle\int\mu_{xc}({\bf r})\rho({\bf r})d^{3}r+{E_{xc}[\rho]},

where ρ\rho is the charge density, VcV_{c} is the Coulombic potential, μx​c\mu_{xc} is the exchange and correlation potential and Ex​cE_{xc} stands for the exchange-correlation energy. The EεE_{\varepsilon} is the sum of eigenvalues

Eε=∑ini​εi,E_{\varepsilon}=\sum_{i}n_{i}{\varepsilon}_{i}, (8)

where εi{\varepsilon}_{i} are eigenvalues of the one-particle Kohn-Sham equation [1]

(T∧+U+Vc+μx​c)​ψi=εi​ψi.(\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\wedge}}{{T}}+U+V_{c}+\mu_{xc})\psi_{i}=\varepsilon_{i}\psi_{i}. (9)

ψi\psi_{i} are self-consistent eigenfunctions, T∧\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\wedge}}{{T}} is operator of kinetic energy and UU stands for pseudopotentials of the ionic sites. The exchange-correlation potential μx​c\mu_{xc} is given in the local density approximation by

μx​c​(𝐫)\displaystyle\mu_{xc}({\bf r}) =\displaystyle= δ​Ex​c​[ρ⁡(𝐫)]δ​ρ​(𝐫)=δ​∫ϵx​c​(𝐫)​ρ​(𝐫)​d3​rδ​ρ​(𝐫)\displaystyle\frac{\delta E_{xc}{[\rho({\bf r})]}}{\delta\rho({\bf r})}=\frac{\delta\int{\epsilon_{xc}({\bf r})~\rho({\bf r})d^{3}r}}{\delta\rho({\bf r})} (10)
=\displaystyle= ϵx​c​(𝐫)+δ​ϵx​c​(𝐫)δ​ρ​(𝐫)​ρ​(𝐫).\displaystyle\epsilon_{xc}({\bf r})+\frac{\delta\epsilon_{xc}({\bf r})}{\delta\rho({\bf r})}\rho({\bf r}).

The variation of Ee​lE_{el} can be then expressed as

δ​Ee​l=\displaystyle\delta E_{el}= δ​∑ini​εi−12​δ​∫ρ⁡(𝐫)​Vc​(𝐫)​d3​r\displaystyle\delta\sum_{i}n_{i}\varepsilon_{i}-\frac{1}{2}\delta\int\rho({\bf r})V_{c}({\bf r})d^{3}r (11)
−\displaystyle- δ​∫δ​ϵx​c​(𝐫)δ​ρ​(𝐫)​ρ​(𝐫)​ρ​(𝐫)​d3​r.\displaystyle\delta\int\frac{\delta\epsilon_{xc}({\bf r})}{\delta\rho({\bf r})}\rho({\bf r})\rho({\bf r})d^{3}r.

The variation of the first term on the right-hand side can be written as

δ​∑ini​εi=∑i[ni​δ​εi+δ​ni​(εi+δ​εi)].\delta\sum_{i}n_{i}\varepsilon_{i}=\sum_{i}{[n_{i}\delta\varepsilon_{i}+\delta n_{i}(\varepsilon_{i}+\delta\varepsilon_{i})]}. (12)

In metallic systems the occupancy can change with an additional potential while in the non-metallic systems the occupation number remains unchanged for small perturbation. Thus, for the non-metallic systems one can write

δ​∑ini​εi=∑ini​δ​εi.\delta\sum_{i}n_{i}\varepsilon_{i}=\sum_{i}n_{i}\delta\varepsilon_{i}. (13)

Having used the perturbation series one obtains

δ​Eε=∑nv​δ​εv=∑v⟨v∣​δ​U+δ​Vc+δ​μx​c​∣v⟩\displaystyle\delta E_{\varepsilon}=\sum n_{v}\delta\varepsilon_{v}=\sum_{v}\langle{v}\mid\delta U+\delta V_{c}+\delta\mu_{xc}\mid{v}\rangle
+∑v,c⟨v∣δ​U+δ​Vc+δ​μx​c∣c⟩​⟨c∣δ​U+δ​Vc+δ​μx​c∣v⟩εv−εc\displaystyle+\sum_{v,c}\frac{\langle{v}\mid\delta U+\delta V_{c}+\delta\mu_{xc}\mid{c}\rangle\langle c\mid\delta U+\delta V_{c}+\delta\mu_{xc}\mid{v}\rangle}{{{\varepsilon}_{v}}-{\varepsilon}_{c}}

+∫ρ0(𝐫)δVc(𝐫)d3r+∫ρ0(𝐫)δμx​c(𝐫)d3r.\displaystyle+\int\rho^{0}({\bf r})\delta V_{c}({\bf r})d^{3}r+\int\rho^{0}({\bf r})\delta\mu_{xc}({\bf r})d^{3}r. (15)

Having used the expression for the variation of the Coulombic potential

Vc​(𝐫)=∫δ​ρ​(𝐫′)|𝐫−𝐫′|​d3​r′,V_{c}({\bf r})=\int\frac{\delta\rho({\bf r^{\prime}})}{|{\bf r-r^{\prime}}|}d^{3}r^{\prime}, (16)

ρ0(𝐫)δVc(𝐫)−12δ(ρ(𝐫)Vc(𝐫))=−12∫δ​ρ​(𝐫)​δ​ρ​(𝐫′)|𝐫−𝐫′|d3r′.\rho^{0}({\bf r})\delta V_{c}({\bf r})-\frac{1}{2}\delta\left(\rho({\bf r})V_{c}({\bf r})\right)=-\frac{1}{2}\int\frac{\delta\rho({\bf r})\delta\rho({\bf r^{\prime}})}{|{\bf r-r^{\prime}}|}d^{3}r^{\prime}. (17)

δ​μx​c​(𝐫)=(δ​μx​c​(𝐫)δ​ρ​(𝐫))0​δ​ρ​(𝐫).\delta\mu_{xc}({\bf r})=\left(\frac{\delta\mu_{xc}({\bf r})}{\delta\rho({\bf r})}\right)_{0}\delta\rho({\bf r}). (22)

∂2Ee​l∂uαμ,0​∂uβν,𝐡|𝐮=𝟎,\left.\frac{\partial^{2}E_{el}}{\partial{u}_{\alpha}^{\mu,0}\partial{u}_{\beta}^{\nu,{\bf h}}}\right|_{\bf{u}=0}, (23)

IV Variation of electron density

The charge density ρ⁡(𝐫)\rho({\bf r}) is calculated from

ρ⁡(𝐫)=∑ini​ψi∗​(𝐫)​ψi​(𝐫),\rho({\bf r})=\sum_{i}n_{i}\psi_{i}^{*}({\bf r})\psi_{i}({\bf r}), (24)

where ni\it{n_{i}} is the occupation number and ψi\psi_{i} are one-electron wavefunctions, the variation of ρ⁡(𝐫)\rho({\bf r}) is expressed as

δρ=∑i(ni+δni)(ψi0∗+δψi∗)(ψi0+δψi)−niψi0∗ψi0.\delta\rho=\sum_{i}(n_{i}+\delta n_{i})(\psi_{i}^{0*}+\delta\psi_{i}^{*})(\psi_{i}^{0}+\delta\psi_{i})-n_{i}\psi_{i}^{0*}\psi_{i}^{0}. (25)

Having supposed that in the non-metallic systems the δ​ni=0\delta n_{i}=0 one can write

δρ=∑ini(ψi0∗δψi+δψi∗ψi0+δψi∗δψi).\delta\rho=\sum_{i}n_{i}(\psi_{i}^{0*}\delta\psi_{i}+\delta\psi_{i}^{*}\psi_{i}^{0}+\delta\psi_{i}^{*}\delta\psi_{i}). (26)

The variation of the wave function

δ​ψi=∑jai​j​ψj0,\delta\psi_{i}=\sum_{j}a_{ij}\psi_{j}^{0}, (27)

and the variation of the electron density can be written as

δ​ρ\displaystyle\delta\rho =\displaystyle= ∑ini∑j(ψi0∗ψj0ai​j+ψj0∗ψi0ai​j∗)\displaystyle\sum_{i}n_{i}\sum_{j}(\psi_{i}^{0*}\psi_{j}^{0}a_{ij}+\psi_{j}^{0*}\psi_{i}^{0}a_{ij}^{*}) (28)
+\displaystyle+ ∑ini∑j​k(ψj0∗ψk0ai​kai​j∗).\displaystyle\sum_{i}n_{i}\sum_{jk}(\psi_{j}^{0*}\psi_{k}^{0}a_{ik}a_{ij}^{*}).

The variation of the wave function is obtained from the Lippmann-Schwinger [12] equation

∣ψi⟩=∣ψi0⟩+G0​(εi)​δ​VK​S​∣ψi⟩,\mid{\psi_{i}}\rangle=\mid{\psi_{i}^{0}}\rangle+G_{0}(\varepsilon_{i})\delta V_{KS}~\mid{\psi_{i}}\rangle, (29)

where G0​(ε)G_{0}(\varepsilon) is the Green function

G0​(ε)=∑i|ψi⟩​⟨ψi|ε−εi,G_{0}(\varepsilon)=\sum_{i}\frac{|\psi_{i}\rangle\langle\psi_{i}|}{\varepsilon-\varepsilon_{i}}, (30)

and δ​VK​S\delta V^{KS} is the variation of the total Kohn-Sham potential

δ​VK​S=δ​U+δ​Vc+δ​μx​c.\delta V^{KS}=\delta U+\delta V_{c}+\delta\mu_{xc}. (31)

With the use of Eqs.(16,22) it can be written as

δ​VK​S=δ​U+∫δ​ρ​(𝐫′)|𝐫−𝐫′|​d3​r′+(δ​μx​c​(𝐫)δ​ρ​(𝐫))0​δ​ρ​(𝐫).\delta V^{KS}=\delta U+\int\frac{\delta\rho({\bf r^{\prime}})}{|{\bf r-r^{\prime}}|}d^{3}r^{\prime}+\left(\frac{\delta\mu_{xc}({\bf r})}{\delta\rho({\bf r})}\right)_{0}\delta\rho({\bf r}). (32)

The elements ai​ja_{ij} are then expressed as

ai​j=⟨ψi0∣δ​ψj⟩=⟨ψi0∣G0​(εi)​δ​VK​S∣ψj0⟩.a_{ij}=\langle\psi_{i}^{0}\mid\delta\psi_{j}\rangle=\langle\psi_{i}^{0}\mid G_{0}(\varepsilon_{i})\delta V_{KS}\mid\psi_{j}^{0}\rangle. (33)

Having combined equations (28) and (33) and applying operator ∂μ,αq\partial_{\mu,\alpha}^{q} which contains the limit to the zero perturbation (Eq.(4)) we obtain integral equation

∂μ,αqρ(𝐫)=∑i,jniψi0∗(𝐫)ψj0(𝐫)\displaystyle\partial_{\mu,\alpha}^{q}\rho({\bf r})=\sum_{i,j}n_{i}\psi_{i}^{0*}({\bf r})\psi_{j}^{0}({\bf r}) (34)
×\displaystyle\times ⟨ψi0∣G0​(εi)​∂μ,αq(U+Vc+μx​c)∣ψj0⟩\displaystyle\langle\psi_{i}^{0}\mid G_{0}(\varepsilon_{i})\partial_{\mu,\alpha}^{q}(U+V_{c}+\mu_{xc})\mid\psi_{j}^{0}\rangle

which can be rewritten into form

∂μ,αqρ⁡(𝐫)\displaystyle\partial_{\mu,\alpha}^{q}\rho({\bf r}) =\displaystyle= ∂μ,αqσ⁡(𝐫)\displaystyle\partial_{\mu,\alpha}^{q}\sigma({\bf r}) (35)
+\displaystyle+ ∫∫Λ⁡(𝐫,𝐫′)​Γ​(𝐫′,𝐫′′)​d3​r′​∂μ,αqρ⁡(𝐫′′)​d3​r′′,\displaystyle\int\int\Lambda({\bf r},{\bf r^{\prime}})\Gamma({\bf r^{\prime}},{\bf r^{\prime\prime}})d^{3}r^{\prime}\partial_{\mu,\alpha}^{q}\rho({\bf r^{\prime\prime}})d^{3}r^{\prime\prime},

where σ\sigma and Λ\Lambda depend only on eigenfunctions and eigenvalues of the unperturbed state. The quantities from previous equation can be expressed as

∂μ,αqσ(𝐫)=∑i,jni−njεi−εjψi0∗(𝐫)ψj0(𝐫)⟨ψj0∣∂μ,αqU∣ψi0⟩\partial_{\mu,\alpha}^{q}\sigma({\bf r})=\sum_{i,j}\frac{n_{i}-n_{j}}{\varepsilon_{i}-\varepsilon_{j}}\psi_{i}^{0*}({\bf r})\psi_{j}^{0}({\bf r})\langle\psi_{j}^{0}\mid\partial_{\mu,\alpha}^{q}U~\mid\psi_{i}^{0}\rangle (36)
Λ(𝐫,𝐫′)=∑i,jni−njεi−εjψi0∗(𝐫)ψj0(𝐫)ψj∗0(𝐫′)ψi0(𝐫′)\Lambda({\bf r},{\bf r^{\prime}})=\sum_{i,j}\frac{n_{i}-n_{j}}{\varepsilon_{i}-\varepsilon_{j}}\psi_{i}^{0*}({\bf r})\psi_{j}^{0}({\bf r})\psi_{j}^{*0}({\bf r^{\prime}})\psi^{0}_{i}({\bf r^{\prime}}) (37)
Γ⁡(𝐫,𝐫′)=1|𝐫′′−𝐫′|+δ⁡(𝐫′−𝐫′′)​(δ​ϵx​c​(𝐫′′)δ​ρ​(𝐫′′))0.\Gamma({\bf r},{\bf r^{\prime}})=\frac{1}{|{\bf r^{\prime\prime}}-{\bf r^{\prime}}|}+\delta({\bf r^{\prime}-r^{\prime\prime}})\left(\frac{\delta\epsilon_{xc}({\bf r^{\prime\prime}})}{\delta\rho({\bf r^{\prime\prime}})}\right)_{0}. (38)

After expansion into plane waves the integral equation (34) yields the set of algebraic equations. By solving this set we obtain ∂μ,αqρ\partial_{\mu,\alpha}^{q}\rho which are used for calculation of the dynamical matrix.

The contribution of the variation of the Ee​lE_{el} to the dynamical matrix is given by the sum of contributions from four terms on the right-hand side of the Eq. (21), i.e.

Dα​βe​l​(𝐪,μ​ν)\displaystyle D_{\alpha\beta}^{el}({\bf q},\mu\nu) =\displaystyle= Dα​βe​l,1​(𝐪,μ​ν)+Dα​βe​l,2​(𝐪,μ​ν)\displaystyle D_{\alpha\beta}^{el,1}({\bf q},\mu\nu)+D_{\alpha\beta}^{el,2}({\bf q},\mu\nu) (39)
+\displaystyle+ Dα​βe​l,3​(𝐪,μ​ν)+Dα​βe​l,4​(𝐪,μ​ν).\displaystyle D_{\alpha\beta}^{el,3}({\bf q},\mu\nu)+D_{\alpha\beta}^{el,4}({\bf q},\mu\nu).

The contribution of the fifth term on the right-hand side of the Eq. (21) is zero because ∂μ,αq∗∂ν,βqΘ(δU+δVc+δμx​c)=0\partial_{\mu,\alpha}^{q*}\partial_{\nu,\beta}^{q}\Theta(\delta U+\delta V_{c}+\delta\mu_{xc})=0.

To calculate the term Dα​βe​l,1​(𝐪,μ​ν)D_{\alpha\beta}^{el,1}({\bf q},\mu\nu) is quite easy because it doesn’t depend on the variation of the charge density δ​ρ\delta\rho but on the variation of the pseudopotential δ​U\delta U only. According to Eqs. (21) one can write

Dα​βe​l,1(𝐪,μν)=∑v,𝐤⟨v,𝐤∣∂μ,αq∗∂ν,βqU∣v,𝐤⟩.D_{\alpha\beta}^{el,1}({\bf q},\mu\nu)=\sum_{v,{\bf k}}\langle{v,{\bf k}}\mid\partial_{\mu,\alpha}^{q*}\partial_{\nu,\beta}^{q}U\mid{v,{\bf k}}\rangle. (40)

More complicated is to calculate Dα​βe​l,2​(𝐪,μ​ν)D_{\alpha\beta}^{el,2}({\bf q},\mu\nu). According to the Eq. (21) one can write

Dα​βe​l,2​(𝐪,μ​ν)=∑v,c,knv,k−nc,k+qεv,k−εc,k+q\displaystyle D_{\alpha\beta}^{el,2}({\bf q},\mu\nu)=\sum_{v,c,k}\frac{n_{v,k}-n_{c,k+q}}{\varepsilon_{v,k}-\varepsilon_{c,k+q}} (41)
×\displaystyle\times ⟨v,𝐤∣∂μ,αq∗(U+Vc+μx​c)∣c,𝐤+𝐪⟩\displaystyle\langle{v,{\bf k}}\mid\partial_{\mu,\alpha}^{q*}(U+V_{c}+\mu_{xc})\mid{c,{\bf k+q}}\rangle
×\displaystyle\times ⟨c,𝐤+𝐪​∣∂ν,βq(U+Vc+μx​c)∣​v,𝐤⟩.\displaystyle\langle{c,{\bf k+q}}\mid\partial_{\nu,\beta}^{q}(U+V_{c}+\mu_{xc})\mid{v,{\bf k}}\rangle.

The sum over v and c in Eq.(41) runs over occupied and unoccupied bands respectively. The Dα​βe​l,3​(𝐪,μ​ν)D_{\alpha\beta}^{el,3}({\bf q},\mu\nu) and Dα​βe​l,4​(𝐪,μ​ν)D_{\alpha\beta}^{el,4}({\bf q},\mu\nu) can be written in the forms

Dα​βe​l,3(𝐪,μν)=−∫∂μ,αq∗ρ(𝐫)∂ν,βqρ(𝐫′)|𝐫−𝐫′|d3rd3r′,D_{\alpha\beta}^{el,3}({\bf q},\mu\nu)=-\int\frac{\partial_{\mu,\alpha}^{q*}\rho({\bf r})\partial_{\nu,\beta}^{q}\rho({\bf r^{\prime}})}{\bf|r-r^{\prime}|}d^{3}rd^{3}r^{\prime}, (42)

and

Dα​βe​l,4(𝐪,μν)=−2∫(δ​ϵx​c​(𝐫)δ​ρ​(𝐫))0∂μ,αq∗ρ(𝐫)∂ν,βqρ(𝐫)d3r.D_{\alpha\beta}^{el,4}({\bf q},\mu\nu)=-2\int\left(\frac{\delta\epsilon_{xc}({\bf r})}{\delta\rho({\bf r})}\right)_{0}\partial_{\mu,\alpha}^{q*}\rho({\bf r})\partial_{\nu,\beta}^{q}\rho({\bf r})d^{3}r. (43)

V Calculations

The calculations were performed with all quantities expanded into plane waves. The set of special 𝐤{\bf k}-points [13, 14] with (18,18,18)(\frac{1}{8},\frac{1}{8},\frac{1}{8}) mesh was used for integration over the Brillouin zone. It corresponds to 10 𝐤{\bf k}-points for Γ\Gamma phonon and 128 𝐤{\bf k}-points for phonon with general wave-vector. The plane-wave set was selected for each 𝐤{\bf k} in the first Brillouin zone such that among the reciprocal-lattice vectors 𝐆{\bf G} only those are selected which have a kinetic energy Ek​i​n=12​(𝐤+𝐆)2E_{kin}=\frac{1}{2}({\bf k+G})^{2} less then Ec​u​t​o​f​f=18​R​yE_{cutoff}=18Ry. The sums over unoccupied states went over energies up to cutoff energy εc​u​t​o​f​f=9​R​y\varepsilon_{cutoff}=9Ry, which corresponds to 350 unoccupied bands approximately.

VI Results

The method presented in this paper was applied to silicon crystal with lattice constant a=0.543​n​ma=0.543~nm. Both optical and acoustic branches of phonon frequencies in longitudinal and transverse modes were obtained for Γ,X\Gamma,X and LL phonons. Calculated frequencies together with values obtained by other authors and experimental values are summarized in Table 1. The values are expressed in T​H​zTHz.

VII Discussion

Having used the presented method a quite good agreement of the calculated frequencies of optical phonons in silicon crystal and experimental ones was reached. We systematically increased the number of unoccupied states taken into account and we have found that the increase over ∼300\sim 300 bands almost doesn’t change the results. Thus, the contribution from states with energy εi>εc​u​t​o​f​f\varepsilon_{i}>\varepsilon_{cutoff} doesn’t appear essential. The biggest individual contributions to the dynamical matrix come from unoccupied states with energy near the Fermi energy. But the number of these states is small, the density of states is approximately g⁡(ε)∼ε1/2g(\varepsilon)\sim\varepsilon^{1/2}, and so it can be said that both dynamical matrix and phonon frequencies are integral quantities where the influence of one state is not essential. Any basis set for sums over unoccupied states is possible but the eigenfunctions of the Kohn-Sham hamiltonian represent the natural choice .

The presented method does not need time consuming calculations of inverse matrix as in the inverse dielectric matrix method. Method of Baroni et al. [5] is based on the self-consistent scheme for perturbed eigenfunctions while our method is based on the self-consistent equation (35) for the variation of the electron density and only energies and eigenfunctions of unperturbed states are needed. King-Smith and Needs [6] used the Hellmann-Feynman forces on all atoms in distorted crystal to construct the dynamical matrix. The method of Gonze et al. [8] is based on variations of the DFT total energy with respect to the first-order perturbations of the wave functions. In this paper, the second derivatives of energy approach is used. The advantage of the presented method is that in contradiction to the both, Baroni et al. method and King-Smith and Needs method, the iteration up to the self-consistency is needed only once for the unpertubed state. In contradiction to the method of Gonze et al., we don’t need any additional minimization of the total energy with respect to the first-order variations of the wave function for each phonon, because all quantities are calculated from quantities of unperturbed state.

Because of avoiding the iterations and minimization the presented method is very suitable for massive parallelization of the computer code.

VIII Conclusion

The method for ab initio calculation of frequency and polarization vector of phonons with an arbitrary wave-vector was presented. The density functional theory within the pseudopotential framework was used. As in other linear response methods, the presented one uses the perturbation theory. In contradiction to the other methods the presented one is based upon a direct calculation of the dynamical matrix via second derivatives of the total crystal energy and no calculation of the Hellman-Feynman forces is needed.

The presented method does not need time consuming calculations of inverse matrix as in the inverse dielectric matrix method. Another advantage is that in contradistinction to the both Baroni et al. [5] method and King-Smith and Needs [6] method, no iteration up to self-consistency for individual phonon is needed. Similarly, we don’t need any total energy minimization as in the case of method of Rignanese, Michenaud and Gonze [7]. The computing time saving due to the parallelization of the computer code is significantly high for the presented method.
